---
title: "Least Squares"
description: "A method for estimating model parameters by minimizing the sum of squared prediction errors."
term: "Least Squares"
letter: "L"
category: "Statistics"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Least squares chooses model parameters so that predictions are, overall, as
close as possible to the observed values, with larger errors penalized more
heavily because they are squared.

## Technical explanation

Given observed targets $y_i$ and predictions $\hat{y}_i(\theta)$, least
squares estimates parameters $\theta$ by minimizing the residual sum of
squares:

$$
\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(y_i - \hat{y}_i(\theta)\right)^2
$$

For a linear model with design matrix $X$, the ordinary least-squares problem
is to minimize $\|y - X\beta\|_2^2$. When $X^\top X$ is invertible, its
solution can be written as $\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$; practical
libraries generally use numerically stable factorizations instead of
explicitly computing this inverse.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Least squares is a foundational fitting method for regression and a useful
reference point for understanding optimization and error metrics. Its
assumptions and sensitivity to outliers matter when selecting a model for
real data.

## How it works

The method calculates residuals (observed minus predicted values), squares
them, and sums them. For linear models, the objective is convex and can be
solved directly or minimized iteratively. Weighted and regularized variants
adapt the objective to different data and constraints.

## Practical example

A team can fit a straight line to historical demand and temperature data to
estimate how demand changes with temperature. Least squares selects the line
with the smallest total squared residual across the training observations.

## Common misconceptions

- Least squares does not guarantee that predictions are accurate outside the data range.
- Squared errors give outliers substantial influence.
- The closed-form equation is not always the most numerically stable way to compute a solution.
